note: Source of truth for FLOW's hack packs. Plain English, no jargon: `problem` is what is wrong, `call` is what somebody could go do about it, `whoFeelsIt` is the person it lands on. Nothing here says what to build. `datasets`/`tools` are places to look, `formats` are shapes other people have used, and `caution` is the one hard limit: it restricts what you may claim, never what you may make. `sources` is generated from `datasets` + `tools` by sync-rewards.py.

efforts.starter: a small first step, an hour or two
efforts.weekend: the whole weekend, better with a mixed team

roles.design: designing how something looks and works
roles.facilitation: running a table, asking people questions

prompts.title: One Gage, One Question
prompts.problem: One machine in the James River posts a new number every fifteen minutes. That is it. One number, over and over, forever.
prompts.call: Take that one number and work out what it can honestly tell somebody, and what it cannot. Every other water problem here is a bigger version of this.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Anyone who has seen a river number and had no idea if it was big or small.
prompts.caution: It is fine to end up saying 'we cannot tell from this.' That is the useful part.

prompts.title: A Year Of The River You Can Hold
prompts.problem: A whole year of river readings is thousands of numbers. On a screen you look at it for two seconds and forget it. If you can hold it, you remember it.
prompts.call: Turn one year of real river numbers into something you can hold, hear, or wear.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone walking past a table who would never click on a chart.
prompts.caution: Say which numbers you smoothed out or left off to make it work.

prompts.title: The Block That Floods And The Block That Hears About It
prompts.problem: Water goes where the ground sends it. Warnings go where mailing lists, phones, and landlords send them. Those are two different maps and they do not match.
prompts.call: Put the two maps side by side and find one place where a person falls through the gap.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A family in the path of the water and not on anybody's warning list.
prompts.caution: Flood maps need careful explaining. Never guess at one household's risk.

prompts.title: The Bill That Explains Nothing
prompts.problem: A water bill is just a number. It does not say which showers or leaks or sprinklers made it that big. It does not say how much you pay no matter what you do. It is the one time most people touch the water system, and it teaches them nothing.
prompts.call: Help someone see what their own habits do to their bill.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A family whose bill doubled, who cannot tell if it is a leak, a price change, or a hot summer.
prompts.caution: Say which numbers you made up or simplified.

prompts.title: I Rent Here. Am I In Trouble?
prompts.problem: Flood information is written for people who own buildings. It talks about parcels, insurance, and elevation. About half of Richmond rents. They get the water and none of the paperwork.
prompts.call: Help a renter find out in one minute whether their place floods, and what to do next.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone about to sign a year-long lease on a ground-floor apartment.
prompts.caution: Flood maps need careful explaining, they are not about one apartment, and people should be pointed to the official source.

prompts.title: Where Does My Rain Go?
prompts.problem: Rain falls on your street and runs away somewhere. Most people have no idea where. The pipes under the road cross lines that nobody ever draws on a map you can see.
prompts.call: Follow the rain from one street all the way to the river, and show the path.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A family whose basement floods and who does not know who to call.
prompts.caution: Maps show where water probably goes. They are not a promise about one house, and real engineering takes more than a map.

prompts.title: The Report Nobody Can Read
prompts.problem: Once a year the city has to tell everyone what is in the drinking water. The paper it sends out is full of words like MCL, turbidity, and parts per million. It follows the law. Nobody reads it.
prompts.call: Turn one page of that report into something a neighbor can actually read.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A parent who just wants to know if the tap water is okay for a baby's bottle.
prompts.caution: You are making it easier to read. You are not testing the water or promising it is safe.

prompts.title: The River Has a Pulse
prompts.problem: Machines in the James River take readings all day long. How fast it flows. How warm it is. How much mud is in it. Almost nobody who swims in it, fishes in it, or lives near it ever sees any of that.
prompts.call: Pick one thing the river tells us and help people understand it.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone who wants to know if it is safe to get in the water today.
prompts.caution: One reading cannot tell you why something happened, or whether the water is safe. Say what you do not know.

prompts.title: One Paragraph, Nobody Understands
prompts.problem: In every city letter, bill, or form there is one paragraph that really matters. It decides if a person acts or gives up. It is usually written for lawyers.
prompts.call: Find one paragraph like that and rewrite it so a kid could follow it. Put both versions side by side.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Anyone who has read an official letter three times and still not known what to do.
prompts.caution: Make the words simpler. Do not change what the person actually has to do.

prompts.title: Eight Panels, One System
prompts.problem: Cities explain themselves with reports and slide decks. The things people actually keep and pass around are comics, zines, and posters on a door. Almost nobody uses those for pipes and buses.
prompts.call: Draw one system in eight panels, from where it starts to somebody's front door.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone who would read eight little pictures and never open a PDF.
prompts.caution: Making it simple is good. Pretending it is simpler than it really is, is not.

prompts.title: Seventy-Two Hours
prompts.problem: Imagine something breaks for three days. Plans for that get written for the whole city. People live it one block at a time: whose tap works, which shop is open, who has a car, who needs power for a machine that keeps them well.
prompts.call: Walk through three days on one block and show what people would need, hour by hour.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A neighbor trying to help a building with no car and no generator.
prompts.caution: This is a made-up story to learn from. It is not a prediction of a real emergency.

prompts.title: Close By, Still Out Of Reach
prompts.problem: Maps tell you how far away a thing is, because that is easy to count. Getting there is a different story. The price. The hours it is open. The bus. A stroller. A wheelchair. A night shift.
prompts.call: Find one place that looks close on a map but is not, and show why.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone whose closest grocery store is a mile away and might as well be ten.
prompts.caution: Being close by does not mean it is cheap, open, or reachable. What you find is a question to look into, not proof.

prompts.title: Who Has A Second Option?
prompts.problem: When something breaks, some people have a backup: another car, a cousin across town, savings, a landlord who picks up the phone. Some people have none. Two streets can lose the same thing and have completely different weeks.
prompts.call: Show which blocks have fewer backups, and be honest about what you cannot see.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A family where one power cut turns into a lost job.
prompts.caution: A number about a whole block says nothing certain about any one person in it. Put that on the map.

prompts.title: Nobody Agrees What Comes First
prompts.problem: There is never enough money to fix water, power, and food all at once. Somebody has to pick. That pick is about what people think matters most. It usually happens in a room with no neighbors in it.
prompts.call: Make a game where people at a table have to make that choice and argue about it.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Residents who only hear about the choice after it has been made.
prompts.caution: Show the trade-offs, and ask whose needs each choice puts first.

prompts.title: The Grid Nobody Can Picture
prompts.problem: Power gets talked about in words nobody uses at home. Megawatt hours. Generation mix. Capacity factors. Between all of that and your light switch there are five or six steps. Nobody ever draws them.
prompts.call: Draw the path from where power is made all the way to one house.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A person who keeps hearing the grid is changing and cannot tell if their bill is part of it.
prompts.caution: A big regional trend does not explain one family's bill or one blackout.

prompts.title: What Is One Row?
prompts.problem: Open any of this data and you get a big pile of rows. The first real question about any of it is what one row is. One house? One reading? One complaint? One guess?
prompts.call: Take data another team is using and write down in plain words what one row means and what it leaves out. Then hand it to them.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: The team three hours in, arguing about a number that turned out to mean something else.
prompts.caution: Describe what is really there, including the parts nobody can explain.

prompts.title: The Bus On Paper And The Bus You Wait For
prompts.problem: A bus schedule is a promise. What you actually get is how often it comes, whether it shows up, how many times you have to change, and whether it runs at the hour you work. The promise is public. The rest is not.
prompts.call: Take one route and show the difference between the paper and the wait.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone whose shift ends after the last useful bus.
prompts.caution: A schedule is not the same as what riders really get.

prompts.title: Counting People Without Watching Them
prompts.problem: Almost every question about a place wants a count: how many people cross here, wait here, come back. The easiest way to count people is also the way that watches them. That is how a neighborhood ends up with cameras nobody asked for.
prompts.call: Build something that counts without knowing who anybody is.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A neighborhood that wants better service and not more cameras.
prompts.caution: Say what your thing is not good enough to claim, and what it deliberately does not collect.

prompts.title: Where Does My Information Go?
prompts.problem: A city form asks for your name, your address, what you earn, a photo of your ID. It almost never says who reads that, how long they keep it, or what else it gets used for. Not knowing is enough to make people stop filling it in.
prompts.call: Show a made-up person's trip through one form, and where the not-knowing stops them.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone who quit an application rather than hand over what it asked for.
prompts.caution: Only ask for things you have a clear reason to ask for.

prompts.title: Reported. Then What?
prompts.problem: You report a pothole, a leak, a broken light. It goes into a system of lists and hand-offs, and out the other end comes either a repair or nothing at all. From outside you cannot tell which one is coming.
prompts.call: Map every hand-off for one kind of report, find where the time goes, and fix one step.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone who reported the same thing three times and gave up.
prompts.caution: Fix one step instead of pretending to replace the whole city system. A slow step is a question to look into, not somebody to blame.

prompts.title: What Actually Moves Through Here
prompts.problem: It is easy to picture a city as places. It is hard to picture it as things moving: water, buses, money, trash, mail, people. Something comes into Richmond, gets handed around, and leaves. Almost none of that is visible.
prompts.call: Pick one thing that moves and follow it all the way through.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Anyone trying to understand a system they are standing inside of.
prompts.caution: Mark which parts you measured, which you guessed, and which you just drew.

prompts.title: What Is On This Block?
prompts.problem: Drains, hydrants, poles, boxes, cracks in the sidewalk. Public stuff is invisible until it breaks, and then nobody knows who to tell.
prompts.call: Walk one block. Find five public things, and work out what each one does and who fixes it.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Anyone who has reported a broken thing to the wrong department.
prompts.caution: If you cannot find out who is responsible, write that down. That gap is the finding.

prompts.title: Digital Infrastructure Is Infrastructure
prompts.problem: Most city services are a website now. A website a screen reader cannot read, or that dies on an old phone or a slow connection, is a locked door with no sign on it. It usually gets treated as a box to tick.
prompts.call: Take one city page or form, find what blocks people, and fix the worst three.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone who cannot use the only way a service is offered.
prompts.caution: You are naming real barriers. You are not certifying a site as accessible.

prompts.title: One Corner, Three Systems
prompts.problem: A street corner is a bus stop, a storm drain, and a repair job all at once. Three different groups run those, with three different lists, and each one only sees its own part. Nobody looks after the corner.
prompts.call: Pick one corner. Look at it three ways and find the question none of them can answer alone.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: The person standing on it, for whom it is just one corner.
prompts.caution: Three partial views do not add up to the truth. Say what each one misses.

prompts.title: Which One Gets Fixed First?
prompts.problem: There are always more broken things than there is money to fix them. So something has to pick the order. That pick is really about whose street comes first. It usually shows up as a score, with no reason given.
prompts.call: Build a way of choosing what gets fixed first that a neighbor could argue with.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A street that has been on the list for six years.
prompts.caution: Easy to explain beats clever. Do not let a model make real repair decisions on its own.

prompts.title: Available Is Not The Same As Connected
prompts.problem: Internet companies say where their wires go. That gets called coverage. But being online also takes money, a contract, a credit check, a device, and knowing how. The official map cannot see any of that.
prompts.call: Show the difference between wires being there and people being online.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A family with three kids, one phone, and homework due tomorrow.
prompts.caution: What providers report is not the same as what people can afford or use.

prompts.title: The Stop With Nothing At It
prompts.problem: Some bus stops have a roof, a bench, a light, and a sidewalk. Others are a sign in the mud beside a road with nowhere to cross. It is often not about how many people use them, and no list says which is which.
prompts.call: Find the stops that need more, and show what makes them different.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone waiting twenty minutes in the rain with a stroller and no curb.
prompts.caution: This points at stops worth a look. A score does not replace somebody going out to check.

prompts.title: The Plan Nobody Can Follow
prompts.problem: Big road and bus projects get decided years ahead, in documents written for agencies and funders. If you want to know what will happen on your street, when, and what it beat out, there is nowhere to look.
prompts.call: Take one project and explain it on one page: what, when, how much, and what it was chosen over.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone whose street is in year four of a plan they have never seen.
prompts.caution: Do not squash real trade-offs into a single score.

prompts.title: One Tract, One Number
prompts.problem: The census cuts the city into small pieces called tracts and publishes numbers about each one. One number about one piece of a city sounds like it says a lot. It says less than you think.
prompts.call: Pick one tract and one number. Work out what it really does and does not tell you about the people living there.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Anyone about to say something big about a neighborhood based on one number.
prompts.caution: One number describes an area, never a household.

prompts.title: Start With What Is Already Here
prompts.problem: Neighborhoods usually get mapped by what they are missing, because that is what brings money in. The churches, corner stores, coaches, and neighbors who already make the place work never get mapped. Then plans get made as if none of that existed.
prompts.call: Map what already works in one neighborhood first. Then add one thing it needs.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: An organizer tired of hearing their neighborhood described as a problem.
prompts.caution: Do not turn a neighborhood into a score for how badly off it is.

prompts.title: How Is This Neighborhood Changing?
prompts.problem: Change shows up in house values, sales, building permits, and census numbers. All of it is public and all of it is late. None of it says what people mean when they say the neighborhood is changing.
prompts.call: Show how one area has changed over time, and say what the records cannot see.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone who has lived on the block for thirty years and is watching it change.
prompts.caution: Never guess whether one family is at risk of being pushed out, based on property or census data.

prompts.title: A Neighborhood Is Not Five Numbers
prompts.problem: Neighborhoods get described with a handful of numbers: money, rent, cars, age, race. Those are the numbers that get published. Everyone who lives there knows the description is thin. The numbers still decide things.
prompts.call: Make one page about one neighborhood, and next to the numbers put what the numbers miss.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A resident who does not recognize their own street in any of the statistics about it.
prompts.caution: A neighborhood is more than its numbers.

prompts.title: Where Do I Even Start?
prompts.problem: A dead streetlight. A question about what can be built next door. A bus that stopped coming. To sort any of it out you have to know which office handles it, what they call it, and what they will ask you for. Knowing that is the hard part, and not everybody does.
prompts.call: Build the front door for one ordinary problem: who handles it, and what they need from you.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A first-time caller who gets transferred twice and hangs up.
prompts.caution: Be clear about which office is responsible and what information they require.

prompts.title: Some Blocks Are Ten Degrees Hotter
prompts.problem: In summer one part of the city can be much hotter than another. It follows lines drawn long ago: where the trees are, where the pavement is, how old the buildings are. The people on the hot blocks already know. They usually do not get asked.
prompts.call: Tell the heat story for one neighborhood, and end with a question for the people who live there.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: A family on a street with no trees in the third week of August.
prompts.caution: Ask residents something before you propose a fix.

prompts.title: Can I Get There Without A Car?
prompts.problem: Richmond is built for driving. Plenty of families have no car. Whether an ordinary trip works without one, like the clinic or a job interview or groceries or court, is not something any map will tell you.
prompts.call: Pick a place people need to get to and show whether you can really get there without a car.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: Someone with a 9am appointment across the river and no car.
prompts.caution: A bus stop nearby does not mean the trip actually works for everybody.

prompts.title: A Partner's Actual Problem
prompts.problem: TEMPLATE. Not ready yet. The projects that keep going after the weekend come from a real group with a real problem they already have.
prompts.call: Organizers: find two or three local groups and write down each one's problem in their own words, one copy of this per group.
prompts.whoFeelsIt: The partner group, who will still have this problem on Monday.
prompts.caution: Do not promise a group ongoing help that nobody has agreed to give.

prompts.title: Build a Fake Water Sensor Responsibly
prompts.problem: Use micro:bit temperature or light inputs, or another simple sensor, to demonstrate time-series environmental sensing and data quality.
prompts.caution: State clearly that the device is not a potable-water testing instrument.

retired.reason: Merged into one responsible-sensing prompt with three worked rigs.

prompts.title: Leak Triage Without the Real Pipes
prompts.problem: Use a synthetic leak and work-order dataset to create a transparent way to decide which reports deserve attention first.
prompts.caution: The model can support discussion; it should not automatically make operational repair decisions.

retired.reason: Same transparent-prioritisation exercise as Which Asset First, on the same synthetic records.

prompts.title: When One System Fails, What Else Moves?
prompts.problem: Model a dependency chain such as power to water pumping to household access, or power to transit signals and mobility.
prompts.caution: Explore assumptions instead of predicting actual outages.

retired.reason: Dependency modelling is too abstract to demo in three days; it is now a mechanic inside the board game.

prompts.title: Find the Missing Link
prompts.problem: Identify a place where retailer access, transit coverage, frequency, and population characteristics suggest a question worth investigating.
prompts.caution: The output is a hypothesis with evidence, not proof that inequity has been established.

retired.reason: Same USDA/GTFS/Census screening as the access prompt.

prompts.title: Find the Bottleneck
prompts.problem: Use a synthetic event log for permits, service requests, buses, queues, or maintenance jobs to visualize where elapsed time accumulates.
prompts.caution: A bottleneck chart should support questions and tests, not assign blame by itself.

retired.reason: Folded into the report-to-repair journey, which already walks the same event log.

prompts.title: Rain To Creek To River
prompts.problem: Build an animated or physical explanation of how water crosses invisible geographic boundaries.
prompts.caution: Keep geographic claims tied to the public watershed source.

prompts.title: Build a Bridge Sensor That Is Not a Bridge Sensor
prompts.problem: Use a micro:bit accelerometer to show how vibration measurements produce time-series data.
prompts.caution: Explain the calibration, engineering knowledge, and validation needed before informing structural decisions.

retired.reason: Merged into one responsible-sensing prompt with three worked rigs.

prompts.title: Maintenance Is Infrastructure
prompts.problem: Given synthetic work orders, create a dashboard about preventive versus reactive maintenance and how different priority rules affect backlog.
prompts.caution: Priority rules are value choices and need public explanation.

retired.reason: Third prompt on the same synthetic work orders; preventive-versus-reactive is now part of the priority model and the repair journey.

prompts.title: Street Speed, Told Clearly
prompts.problem: Use Richmond public speed information to create a resident-facing explanation of what the data show and which patterns deserve questions.
prompts.caution: The dashboard cannot establish every cause or intervention by itself.

retired.reason: No confirmed dataset behind 'Richmond public speed information'; highest dead-end risk in the set. Restore once a specific dataset is pinned.

prompts.title: Flood Information by Neighborhood
prompts.problem: Translate regional flood-risk information into a neighborhood-specific civic guide for renters, property owners, and official resources.
prompts.caution: Explain what the map tells you and what it does not.

retired.reason: Duplicate of the renter-facing flood prompt; one flood explainer is enough.
